title: How to Reduce PDF File Size Without Losing Readability
excerpt: A practical compression workflow that checks small text, page counts and selectable text instead of promising a fixed saving.
seoDescription: A practical compression workflow that checks small text, page counts and selectable text instead of promising a fixed saving.
author: The MY PDF FIX Team
body:
## Decide what must survive compression

A readable PDF is not necessarily a searchable or accessible PDF. Turning a page into an image can make the words look acceptable while removing selectable text, links and form fields. Before reducing size, decide whether the recipient needs those features as well as a readable page.

[Compress PDF](/compress-pdf) provides Light, Recommended and Strong. Light resaves the PDF without rasterizing pages. Recommended and Strong also try an image-based version and choose a smaller result. The output may therefore be a rasterized copy, a lossless resave or the original when a worthwhile reduction is unavailable. No percentage saving or maximum attachment size is guaranteed.

## Work an attachment-limit example

Suppose a portal accepts at most 5 MB and your report is larger. The limit is an example; check the actual portal's instructions and units before proceeding.

1. Keep the original and note its size, page count and important interactive features.
2. Remove genuinely unnecessary pages with [Remove Pages](/remove-pdf-pages), if your submission rules allow it. Do not omit required evidence merely to hit a size limit.
3. Open [Compress PDF](/compress-pdf), choose Light first if selectable text matters, then click **Process**.
4. Read the result's size note and download it. Check the saved file's actual size rather than assuming a success message means the portal will accept it.
5. If it is still too large, return to the original and try Recommended. Inspect the result before choosing Strong.
6. If a readable file still exceeds the limit, consider [splitting by page ranges](/split-pdf) only if multiple attachments are permitted. Otherwise ask the recipient for an alternative submission method.

This process describes decisions to make; it does not claim a particular reduction for your document.

## Inspect the parts most likely to suffer

Check the smallest footnote, a thin line on a chart, a faint stamp and any colored legend. Zoom in, but also inspect at the intended reading or print size. An image that looks fine on a phone may not reproduce small handwriting clearly on paper.

Search for a known phrase and copy a sentence that was selectable in the original. Open a link and inspect filled form values. Count pages. Rasterized outputs can preserve visible appearances while losing the structure that made these actions work.

## Common mistakes

Repeatedly compressing successive outputs compounds image degradation. Compare each candidate with the original. Do not treat grayscale as an automatic file-size fix: [Grayscale PDF](/grayscale-pdf) rasterizes pages and may increase a compact text PDF's size.

Avoid an arbitrary “best DPI” rule for every document. Dense diagrams, scanned handwriting and ordinary typed text have different needs. This interface offers preset levels rather than per-image optimization controls.

## If the size barely changes or processing fails

An already optimized file may offer little saving. A small text-only PDF can even become larger when rendered as images, which is why the tool compares candidates. A result that does not shrink is not necessarily a malfunction.

Large page counts and high-resolution images consume browser memory. Close unnecessary tabs or try fewer pages on a device with more available memory. There is no guaranteed maximum file size, and reducing a PDF's on-disk size does not directly measure the memory needed to render it.

## Frequently asked questions

**Can I guarantee no quality loss?** Light avoids rasterization, but always review the result. Recommended and Strong can trade structure and detail for size.

**Why can I no longer highlight text?** The chosen result may contain page images. Return to the original and use Light if text selection is required.

**Will a smaller PDF pass every portal?** No. Portals can also impose page-size, encryption, version or naming requirements. Read those separately.

For the distinction between scans and embedded text, see [extracting text and recognizing scanned pages](/blog/extract-text-and-recognize-scanned-pdfs).
